summary: On September 15, 2023, the city council passed sweeping zoning law changes meant to expand and diversify housing. The changes up-zone areas for higher density, cut parking requirements, and add inclusionary zoning for affordable housing, with implementation phased through late 2025. Supporters cite affordability, economic growth, and sustainability, while some residents worry about gentrification and neighborhood character.
one_line: The city council passed zoning reforms on September 15, 2023, allowing higher density, less parking, and mandatory affordable housing, with phased rollout through late 2025.
key_facts: The city council passed the new zoning laws on September 15, 2023, after a meeting that lasted several hours.
City Planner Emily Rodriguez presented the proposal, which up-zones certain areas for higher density housing, reduces parking requirements, and adds 'inclusionary zoning' policies.
Inclusionary zoning requires a set percentage of new construction to be allocated for affordable housing.
Affordable housing is often defined in the note as housing that costs no more than 30% of a household's income.
Councilmember Brian Thomas said implementation will be progressive, ending with completion of compliant housing developments by late 2025.
Councilmember Janice Liu hopes the inclusionary zoning requirement will make a severe dent in the affordable housing shortage.
Density increases are particularly aimed at neighborhoods traditionally zoned for single-family homes.
A strip of Manchester Avenue, currently mostly low-rise commercial buildings, could become an enclave of mixed-use buildings with retail and residences.
Transport Committee Chair Lisa Gomez defended reduced parking requirements, saying 'We're reimagining our urban landscape in a way that prioritizes people, not cars.'
Local economist Michael Chen reported to the council that the changes could significantly boost economic activity by attracting investment and increasing the local tax base.
Resident John Avery supported affordable housing and mixed-zone areas, while community advocate Marisa Lopez raised concerns about gentrification and preservation of neighborhood character.
City Council President Angela Martinez said community input will continue to shape the approach through ongoing workshops and hearings.
The laws encourage green building practices, energy-efficient construction, reduced urban sprawl, and maintained green spaces.
The council plans to review zoning impacts regularly and adjust regulations as needed.
